paragraphs: The following assessments concern character makeup work by theatrical and performance makeup artists. They do not predict hiring, qualifications, authorization, or contract outcomes.

The core work of theatrical and performance makeup artists is to design and apply makeup that reflects a performer's character, period, and setting: analyze scripts and note events affecting character appearance, research character descriptions and period materials, review sketches, photographs, and plaster models, consult directors and performers on effects, assess skin types and lighting and locations, mix greasepaint and pigments or select ready-made shades, attach prosthetics and create special effects such as scars, aging, and illness, modify and maintain makeup during filming for continuity, write makeup charts and photograph product records, request wigs, beards, and other materials and work within budgets, assist makeup removal, and wash and style wigs.

Entirely fictional task package: provide a fictional character and scene brief, including 1 set of character appearance points, 1 period makeup reference, and 1 filming continuity requirement. Within 60 minutes, write a makeup plan, materials and colors, skin and safety assessment, and continuity maintenance and documentation methods. Do not use real production, actor, or creative work data.

Sample output and reflection: check whether you first analyzed character and period materials, explained material and color choices, assessed skin and safety, and provided continuity maintenance and documentation methods. Then ask whether you can remain attentive under filming schedules and time pressure, and whether you are willing to take responsibility for makeup effects and actor skin safety.

This page covers O*NET 39-5091.00 theatrical and performance makeup artists: applying makeup to performers to reflect their characters' periods, settings, and situations. Work includes script analysis and production research, reviewing sketches, photographs, and plaster models, creating character drawings or models, consulting directors and performers, assessing skin and lighting, selecting or mixing makeup, attaching prosthetics and creating special effects, modifying and maintaining makeup during production for continuity, requesting materials and budgeting, writing makeup charts and taking photographs, demonstrating products and providing instruction, assisting makeup removal, and washing wigs. Work mainly takes place at rehearsals and filming locations. This page excludes adjacent roles such as skincare specialists, wardrobe attendants, and art designers.

entries: Inputs: scripts and character descriptions, period and production reference materials, sketches, photographs and plaster models, makeup materials such as greasepaint, creams, pigments, and prosthetics, wigs and beards, makeup tools and cleaning supplies, performer skin and lighting and location information, makeup charts, and budget forms.

Inspectable outputs: makeup consistent with character and period, special effects and prosthetic looks, makeup continuity and modification records, makeup charts and look photographs, budget and purchasing records, product demonstration and instruction records, and makeup removal and wig cleaning and maintenance results.

Complete workflow: analyze scripts and research period materials → consult directors and performers and finalize plans → assess skin, lighting, and locations → mix or select makeup and prepare materials → complete base makeup, special effects, and prosthetics → modify and maintain continuity during filming → record makeup charts, assist removal, and maintain wigs.

paragraphs: Key judgments: whether makeup fits the character, period, and director's intent, whether materials and colors are appropriate and tolerable for the skin, how to attach effects and prosthetics safely, how to maintain filming continuity, and how to balance budgets with material availability.

Environment and pace: mainly rehearsal and filming locations, with hours varying by production schedules, potentially involving early starts, late finishes, and extended work. Work requires prolonged standing and fine hand movements, contact with makeup materials and actors' skin, and time pressure from continuity and on-site changes.

Research inputs: occupational identity, tasks, work activities, work context, skills and knowledge, interest code, education, and Job Zone for O*NET 39-5091.00. Pay, employment, and industry data on that page cover this occupation. These findings do not establish mainland Chinese qualifications, wages, or employment categories.

Check first: character and period requirements, director intent and filming plans, actor skin and allergies, lighting and location conditions, material and budget limits, and safety and hygiene requirements.

Work cycle: begin with script analysis and research, continue through consultation and final plans, skin and lighting assessment, makeup mixing and material preparation, base makeup and effects, and finish with continuity modifications, makeup charts, removal assistance, and maintenance. Do not finalize makeup before skin safety and character requirements are confirmed or finish the day's work before continuity issues are handled.

Boundaries with adjacent duties: this page covers only theatrical and performance makeup artists. Skincare specialists provide routine skincare and beauty services, wardrobe attendants handle clothing, and art designers handle overall visuals. Hairstyling, costumes, and overall art direction must not be treated as interchangeable with this role.

Skincare specialists provide routine skincare and beauty treatments. Theatrical and performance makeup artists design and apply makeup consistent with character periods and settings; purposes and clients differ.
Wardrobe attendants organize, coordinate, and maintain costumes. Theatrical and performance makeup artists handle makeup and prosthetics. The roles often collaborate but deliver different objects.
Art designers handle overall visuals and scene styles. Theatrical and performance makeup artists focus on character makeup and effects, creating character appearances within the art design.
Actors perform characters. Theatrical and performance makeup artists create their character appearances, communicating with actors about skin feel and comfort and supporting performance needs.

Human control points include assessing skin and safety, mixing makeup to character and period requirements, safely attaching prosthetics, maintaining filming continuity, and taking responsibility for makeup effects and actor skin safety.

Start with an offline exercise using an entirely fictional character and scene brief. Record makeup plans, materials and colors, and safety boundaries, without relying on unverified automated generation to replace on-site confirmation.

Editorial trial suggestion: a small sample draft using fictional materials only. Ordinary dedicated software differs from generative AI; widespread organizational adoption in this occupation has not been established.
Follow character requirements, skin safety, and hygiene procedures, retaining human judgment and records.

Fit signals: start with observable work behavior

To assess fit, first consider whether you can turn written characters into specific makeup looks, communicate patiently with actors and address skin and allergies, maintain continuity under filming schedules and time pressure, document attentively and collaborate, and take responsibility for makeup effects and skin safety. Tools such as RIASEC can only suggest hypotheses and cannot replace real task experience.
Positive signals: turning characters into makeup plans, patient communication and attention to skin safety, maintaining continuity under time pressure, and documentation and collaboration.

Reasons for caution: difficulty translating written characters into visual plans, reluctance to communicate patiently and assess skin, difficulty maintaining continuity under filming schedules and on-site changes, or inability to follow hygiene and safety requirements.

Trial activity: use an entirely fictional character and scene brief to practice makeup planning, material and color choices, skin safety assessment, and continuity records. Ask another person to review the records.

The RIASEC interest code is AR, Artistic–Realistic: a preference for creating visual looks and applying makeup effects by hand. These labels describe activity preferences only and cannot determine competence or qualifications.

General personality scales such as the Big Five do not provide job evidence for this occupation and may be used only for self-reflection. Continue checking against real makeup design, on-site execution, and communication experience.
Type tools such as MBTI and the Enneagram cannot determine competence or qualifications and may be used only for self-reflection.

Entry paths and stages of capability

O*NET Job Zone3 descriptions of vocational schooling, experience, associate degrees, and training durations are general group information, not uniform occupational thresholds. Surveyed education for this occupation lists 33% high school, 29% postsecondary certificates, and 10% below high school, with the remainder outside these three categories. Check production and specific jurisdiction requirements; do not promise entry within one to two years.

Editorial suggestion: compare actual tasks and costs of school training, assistant practice, and supervised production experience. No pathway proportions or evidence of portfolio versus certificate hiring weight were obtained. No one-to-one Chinese qualification mapping for 39-5091.00 has been established. Check makeup services, product operations, and other actual activities separately; do not assume one credential applies to all workers.

Training certificates, professional certification, and business qualifications are different statuses. Training does not automatically confer practice or business qualifications. For skin handling and cosmetic use, check local jurisdiction and employer authorization requirements.

Entry stage: practice base makeup and cleaning, observe on-site workflows, organize materials and makeup charts, and learn skin and hygiene safety procedures under supervision, retaining process records.

Evidence to show: provide a reviewable portfolio and records, including character analysis, makeup plans, materials and colors, and on-site photographs, to demonstrate makeup execution and documentation according to character and period requirements.

Next step: check the target production or institution's character needs, filming workflows, material and budget limits, and skin and hygiene requirements. Validate on-site execution and continuity skills through supervised real projects.

Moving toward greater responsibility: with experience, workers may become lead makeup artists, handle character look development and team mentoring, or move into special effects prosthetics, film and television look design, and teaching.

Moving into skincare services requires separate skincare service procedures, skin and product knowledge, hygiene management, target jurisdiction qualifications, and service boundaries. Character makeup experience does not confer skincare service or medical diagnosis and treatment authority.

career_risk_cards.heading: Work risks and boundaries for theatrical and performance makeup artists

risks.consequence: May cause allergies or skin irritation.
risks.mitigation: Check product uses, ingredients, and actor feedback. Stop for abnormalities; a makeup trial does not guarantee no allergy. For eye irritation, follow FDA advice to stop use and seek medical help for persistent discomfort. Makeup artists do not diagnose or independently treat conditions.
risks.scenario: Using makeup materials without skin assessment.

risks.mitigation: Follow use procedures and maintain ventilation and protection.
risks.scenario: Using solvents or materials without ventilation and protection.

risks.consequence: May cause skin damage and discomfort.
risks.mitigation: Follow the product's intended body areas, manufacturer attachment / removal methods, and trained procedures. Stop and refer pain or irritation. Eye-specific guidance cannot be extended to all prosthetics; do not forcibly peel them off.
risks.scenario: Improper prosthetic attachment or removal methods.

risks.consequence: May affect the finished production and consistency of effects.
risks.mitigation: Document and review using makeup charts and photographs.
risks.scenario: Failure to detect on-site continuity issues promptly.

risks.mitigation: Assess needs early and schedule and prepare materials reasonably.

risks.consequence: May cause infection and hygiene risks.
risks.mitigation: Keep hands, containers, and eye tools clean. Do not share eye cosmetics or use them on inflamed or infected areas. Follow on-site hygiene procedures to prevent cross-contamination between actors.
risks.scenario: When tools are not cleaned or shared without disinfection.
risks.title: Cross-contamination from inadequate hygiene

source_card.note: Check source scope, limitations, and statistical periods separately against original evidence. Source usage notes: O*NET 39-5091.00 Makeup Artists, Theatrical and Performance (Summary) provides occupational identity, official description, interest code, Job Zone, skills, and knowledge for 39-5091.00. Pay and employment data on that page cover this occupation. O*NET 39-5091.00 Tasks provides tasks including script analysis and research, consultation and final plans, skin and lighting assessment, makeup mixing, prosthetics and special effects, continuity, makeup charts, budgets, and purchasing. The task sample does not imply that every job performs all tasks. O*NET 39-5091.00 Work Context describes on-site work, material and skin contact, time pressure and continuity, prolonged standing, and fine operations. US work context does not replace Chinese law or employer procedures. O*NET 39-5091.00 National Wages (BLS OEWS display) provides 2025 BLS OEWS median pay for this occupation. This page does not display pay percentiles. O*NET 39-5091.00 National Employment Trends provides 2024 employment and projections for growth and openings during 2024–2034. Projections do not guarantee hiring. Industries: 39-5091.00 lists Information as the main industry in 2024. Industry distribution signals employer settings, not projected growth or demand. O*NET 39-5091.00 Education and Job Preparation: Job Zone 3, most jobs require vocational school training, related experience or an associate degree, plus one to two years of training. The education distribution does not establish a mandatory requirement for every employer. National Certifications: 39-5091.00 is the US national certification lookup provided by O*NET. Certification and training do not establish practice or business qualifications. Generative AI and Jobs (ILO Working Paper 140, 2025) assesses occupational exposure to generative AI at the task level. The exposure index does not equal adoption rates, job outcomes, or hiring probabilities. Average Annual Wages of Employees in Urban Units in 2025 provides average annual wages by industry category for urban nonprivate and private units, including culture, sports, and entertainment. Industry averages are not occupational medians and exclude individual businesses and freelancers. Enterprise Remuneration Survey Information (2024) from the Ministry of Human Resources and Social Security is a pay lookup organized by occupation / position. It covers urban enterprises, excluding government agencies and public institutions; this page did not obtain an entry precisely matching this occupation. The FermatMind Task Impact Scale for Theatrical and Performance Makeup Artists organizes tasks that tools may assist and human control points for task-level AI and fit discussion. The editorial scale is not evidence of adoption rates, layoffs, regulations, or credentials.

description.text: This page covers O*NET 39-5091.00 theatrical and performance makeup artists: applying makeup to film, television, and stage performers to reflect character periods and settings, analyzing scripts and period materials, assessing skin and lighting, mixing makeup, attaching prosthetics and creating special effects, maintaining filming continuity, recording makeup charts, and assisting removal. To assess this career path, verify the work cycle, skin safety and authorization boundaries, evidence scope, risk controls, and observable beginner work samples together.

subject.summary: This page covers O*NET 39-5091.00 theatrical and performance makeup artists: applying makeup to performers to reflect their characters' periods, settings, and situations, including script analysis and production research, consultation with directors and performers, makeup mixing, prosthetics and special effects, maintaining continuity, and recording makeup charts.
